# Ethnographic Journal: Santiago, November 2025

**Location**: Multiple offices and public spaces, Santiago, Chile  
**Duration**: 2 weeks embedded observation  
**Date**: November 1-14, 2025

---

## Personal Reflection: The Researcher Adapts

I stopped drinking coffee myself 3 weeks ago to better understand participants. The first week was hell - headaches, fatigue, irritability. By week two, something shifted. I sleep better. I wake naturally. My energy is lower but more stable.

I wonder if my entire adult life has been artificially sped up.

## Week 1: First Impressions

Santiago has fully adapted. Siesta culture, which was losing ground to "American-style" work culture, has returned with force.

Offices open 9am. Work until 1pm. Long lunch/siesta 1-4pm. Work 4-7pm. Nobody questions this. It is just how life works now.

Watched Pablo (software company CEO) explain: "We tried to fight it. Tried to keep 9-5 schedule. People were miserable, productivity tanked. So we gave in. Siesta is not laziness. It is adaptation to reality of human energy without stimulants."

## Week 1: The Afternoon Rest

Followed Valentina (designer, 32) through her day:

9am: Arrives fresh, focused. Morning work is intense, concentrated. "I do my best work now," she says. "My mind is clear."

1pm: Long lunch with colleagues. They walk to restaurant, eat slowly, talk about life. No phones on table. Two hours.

3pm: Valentina goes home (lives nearby) and naps. "20 minutes, sometimes 40. I wake naturally."

4pm: Returns to office. Slower pace but steady. Reviews morning work, responds to messages, meets with team.

7pm: Leaves office. Evening is for family, friends, hobbies.

Valentina: "Before collapse, I worked 9-7 straight through, grabbed sandwich at desk, came home exhausted, watched TV, slept, repeated. I was productive but miserable. Now I work less hours but I am... happy? Is that allowed?"

## Week 1: Social Renaissance

The streets are alive in early evening. People walking, talking, sitting in cafes (serving tea, juice, food - no coffee anywhere).

Plazas that were empty during work hours now fill 6-8pm. Families, friends, colleagues.

Carlos (teacher, 45): "We have time now. Before, we were always rushing. Work, home, sleep, repeat. Now we actually live. I know my neighbors. I play with my children. We have dinner together every night."

## Week 2: Productivity Paradox

Interviewed 8 companies about output:

Consistent pattern: hours worked down 40-50%. Output down 20-30%. But profitability stable or improved.

Why? Less rework. Better quality. Lower burnout/turnover. Fewer sick days.

Maria (operations manager): "Before, people worked 50 hours to produce 40 hours of good work. Rest was mistakes, churn, burnout. Now they work 30 hours and produce 35 hours of good work. Somehow we are more efficient."

## Week 2: The Death of Hustle Culture

Pablo (CEO): "Nobody brags about working long hours anymore. It is embarrassing, like admitting you cannot manage your time. The flex now is work-life balance."

LinkedIn post from tech worker went viral: "Closed 3 major deals this month working 25 hours/week. No burnout. Home for dinner with family every night. This is the dream."

## Week 2: Children and Families

Visited 3 families for dinner observations:

Children have parents present. Dinners last 90 minutes with conversation. Homework gets help. Bedtime stories are normal, not luxury.

Sofía (mother of 2): "Before collapse, I saw my kids 2 hours a day. Breakfast rush, bedtime rush. I was coffee-fueled zombie. Now I am tired, yes, but I am HERE. I am present. They have their mother back."

## Week 2: The Black Market That Never Came

Expected to find underground coffee trade. Found almost nothing.

Few people still chasing coffee (expensive, poor quality, unreliable). Most have moved on.

Luis (former coffee addict): "I tried black market coffee last month. It cost 10x normal price and tasted like dirt. I drank it and felt... wired. Anxious. Could not sleep that night. I realized I do not want that feeling anymore. I like being calm."

## Week 2: Health Observations

Spoke with Dr. Ramírez, general practitioner:

"Anxiety cases down 40%. Sleep disorder cases down 60%. People are sleeping 8-9 hours naturally. Blood pressure down across population. Stress hormones lower.

But yes, people are tired during day. They move slower. But they are not sick. Just... running at human speed instead of artificial speed."

## Final Reflection: Were We The Addicts?

Sitting in plaza at sunset, watching families gather, children playing, people talking slowly over tea.

Everyone looks tired. But they also look... content?

Valentina said something that stays with me: "We thought coffee made us productive. But maybe it just made us tolerate being unproductive? We could work long hours because we were stimulated, but we were not actually working better. Just working more."

The collapse felt like catastrophe in July. By September, adaptation. Now in November, it feels like... liberation?

People work less. Produce nearly as much. Live more. Connect more. Sleep better. Stress less.

The question nobody wants to ask: What if this is better?

What if the coffee era was the anomaly - a brief period where humanity ran on stimulants and called it progress? What if this is what human life is supposed to look like?

I watch the plaza. People laughing, talking, living. Moving at human pace.

Maybe we were the addicts all along.

---

## Research Conclusions:

The Great Coffee Collapse of 2025 was not the end of productivity. It was the end of productivity theater.

Without caffeine, humans cannot maintain artificial urgency. But we can maintain focus, quality, and purpose - just in different rhythms.

The cost: lower output (20-30%), slower pace, mandatory rest periods.

The benefit: better quality work, lower stress, deeper relationships, healthier population, actual work-life balance.

Society is not collapsing. It is adapting. And many people prefer the adaptation to what came before.
